# Osteonecrosis of the femoral head

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > Lower extremity > Osteonecrosis of the femoral head*

[Original Article Link](/library/5Q0i9f)

---

## Summary

<u>Osteonecrosis</u> of the femoral head is a consequence of insufficient vascular supply to the femoral head. Most cases are either <u>idiopathic</u> or associated with <u>alcohol</u>, <u>corticosteroid</u> therapy, or trauma. The condition manifests with groin <u>pain</u>, which may radiate to the knee or <u>ipsilateral</u> buttock, and a limited <u>range of motion</u> at the hip. Diagnosis is based on <u>x-ray</u>, followed by <u>MRI</u>. No curative treatments have been identified and there is no consensus on the best treatment options. Initial nonsurgical treatment focuses on preventing collapse of the femoral head, but surgical treatment is commonly required. <u>Core decompression</u> may improve the prognosis in early stages. If the disease progresses, <u>arthroplasty</u> may be necessary.




For <u>avascular necrosis</u> of the femoral head in children, see “<u>Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease</u>.”

---

## Epidemiology

* Peak <u>incidence</u>: 20–40 years [[1]](/library/vk0ApT)



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

Though often <u>idiopathic</u>, several traumatic and atraumatic factors may contribute to the development of <u>osteonecrosis</u>.




* Atraumatic factors  [[1]](/library/vk0ApT)[[2]](/library/9k0NJT)

* <u>Glucocorticoid</u> use (35–40% of cases)

* <u>Alcohol use disorder</u> (20–40% of cases)

* <u>Legg-Calvé-Perthes</u>

* Smoking

* <u>Hemoglobinopathies</u> (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>)

* Radiation

* <u>Myeloproliferative disorders</u>

* Autoimmune diseases (e.g., <u>SLE</u>, <u>antiphospholipid syndrome</u>)

* <u>Hyperuricemia</u>, <u>hyperlipoproteinemia</u>, <u>diabetes mellitus</u>

* <u>Pancreatitis</u>

* Infection

* <u>Gaucher disease</u>

* <u>Decompression sickness</u>

* Traumatic factors 

* <u>Femoral neck fractures</u>, particularly with <u>dislocation</u> [[1]](/library/vk0ApT)

* <u>Femoral head fracture</u>

* <u>Slipped capital femoral epiphysis</u> (<u>SCFE</u>)





> [!NOTE]
> ASEPTIC: Alcohol, Sickle cell disease/S<u>LE</u>, Exogenous <u>steroid</u>, Pancreatitis, Trauma, Infection, Caisson disease (<u>decompression sickness</u>)

---

## Pathophysiology

* Reduced blood supply and <u>bone marrow</u> <u>infarction</u>

* The femoral head is at particular risk of developing <u>avascular necrosis</u> because there is an area of reduced vascularization (<u>watershed zone</u>) between the <u>cranial</u> and <u>caudal</u> parts.  

* The <u>cranial</u> part receives blood from a branch of the <u>obturator artery</u>.

* The <u>caudal</u> part receives blood from <u>medial</u> and <u>lateral femoral circumflex arteries</u>.

* The <u>foveolar artery</u> is the main <u>artery</u> implicated in <u>avascular necrosis</u> of the femoral head

* Most commonly originates from the <u>obturator artery</u> and less commonly from the <u>medial circumflex femoral artery</u> [[3]](/library/ZiXZJB)

* Passes through the <u>ligament</u> of the <u>femur</u> head

* Supplies the head of the <u>femur</u>




![Arteries of the femoral head with watershed zone](media/ai2m020bw2c0tapygg2hcq1v.jpg)

Arteries of the femoral head with watershed zone

---

## Clinical features

* Slowly progressive groin <u>pain</u>, which may radiate to the knee or <u>ipsilateral</u> buttock  [[4]](/library/zr1rPR0)

* Limited active and passive <u>range of motion</u> at the hip

* Bilateral in 40–80% of cases [[4]](/library/zr1rPR0)





> [!TIP]
> Consider <u>osteonecrosis</u> in patients presenting with groin <u>pain</u> and a history of <u>corticosteroid</u> use or <u>alcohol use disorder</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

Diagnostic studies are used to rule out other causes of <u>hip pain</u> and allow for early detection and implementation of treatments to prevent and/or slow disease progression. [[4]](/library/zr1rPR0)




### Imaging [[5]](/library/O1WIS40)[[6]](/library/Y1Wn240)




* <u>X-ray</u>: best initial test   [[5]](/library/O1WIS40); 

* Recommended views: AP, <u>frog-leg lateral</u>, and oblique

* Findings  [[7]](/library/F_1gJj0)[[8]](/library/Lz1wtj0)

* Cystic and <u>sclerotic</u> changes in the femoral head

* Subchondral collapse

* Flattening of the femoral head

* Crescent sign: curvilinear subchondral line in the <u>proximal</u> femoral head

* <u>MRI</u>: <u>confirmatory test</u> 

* Study of choice for early detection in clinically suspected cases with or without suspicious <u>x-ray</u> findings

* Findings   [[5]](/library/O1WIS40)

* Visualization of the interface between <u>necrotic</u> and viable bone

* <u>Bone marrow</u> <u>edema</u>, <u>joint effusion</u>

* May show asymptomatic <u>osteonecrosis</u> of the <u>contralateral</u> hip

* CT: superior to <u>MRI</u> for detecting <u>insufficiency fractures</u>; also used for preoperative planning [[5]](/library/O1WIS40)





> [!TIP]
> In patients with <u>sickle cell anemia</u> and <u>osteonecrosis</u> of the hip, consider evaluating for <u>osteonecrosis</u> of other <u>joints</u>. [[9]](/library/tz1Xuj0)

### Staging




There are several staging systems for <u>osteonecrosis</u> of the femoral head; in general, the following four important findings are used to assess severity:




* Evidence of bone collapse or impending bone collapse

* Size of the <u>necrotic</u> component

* Amount of femoral head <u>depression</u>

* <u>Acetabular</u> involvement

---

## Treatment

Nonoperative management can provide relief in early stages of the disease, but operative treatment is usually necessary for most patients.




* Nonoperative management: for symptomatic relief in early disease stages and patients who are not surgical candidates [[4]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[6]](/library/Y1Wn240)[[8]](/library/Lz1wtj0)

* Avoid <u>weight-bearing</u> on the affected side to prevent femoral head collapse.

* Address <u>risk factors</u>: e.g., smoking, <u>alcohol</u> use, <u>corticosteroid</u> use (if feasible)

* Pharmacological treatments are sometimes used, but there is a paucity of evidence on their <u>efficacy</u>.

* Surgical treatment: may improve prognosis if performed in early stages [[4]](/library/zr1rPR0)[[8]](/library/Lz1wtj0)[[10]](/library/-RXDpB)

* Interventions to prevent collapse of the femoral head

* Core decompression: decompressing the femoral head to restore normal vascular flow

* Bone graft to fill <u>necrotic</u> areas

* <u>Osteotomy</u> to redistribute weight load

* Reconstructive procedures

* Resurfacing <u>arthroplasty</u>

* <u>Hemiarthroplasty</u>

* <u>Total hip arthroplasty</u>
